whyWrong.C: Has the same splice as the first option and additionally leaves "on the contrary" unpunctuated on its left.

whyCorrect: The subject is "the number," not "states and territories" — everything after of modifies it. "The number" is singular, and the sentence describes something that happens repeatedly in the present, "almost every year," so the simple present singular shrinks is the form that fits.

whyWrong.B: Plural, so it agrees with the nouns inside the modifying phrase rather than with the head noun of the subject.
whyWrong.C: Also plural, and the progressive describes an action in progress rather than a recurring yearly change.
whyWrong.D: Plural as well, and the present perfect progressive does not sit well with the repeated-event marker "almost every year."

commonMistakes: Confusing "the number of" with "a number of"; the first is singular, the second takes a plural verb.

whyCorrect: The relative clause introduced by that already has its verb waiting at the far end of the blank: emphasizes. So whatever fills the blank cannot be a second finite verb; it has to be a modifying phrase inserted between the relative pronoun and its verb. "That, aiming to teach music in the same natural way children learn language, emphasizes …" does that, with commas closing the insertion on both sides.

whyWrong.A: Places a comma between that and a conjugated verb, which no relative clause allows.
whyWrong.C: Supplies a second finite verb, so the clause ends up with aims and emphasizes joined by a comma and no conjunction.
whyWrong.D: Has the same two-verb problem; changing the tense does not remove the missing conjunction.

whyCorrect: The techniques belong to the guild, and the first clause names exactly one: "The weavers guild kept its patterns secret." A singular noun takes an apostrophe before the s, giving guild's techniques.

whyWrong.A: Is a plain plural with no apostrophe, so it shows no possession and also multiplies a guild the passage keeps singular.
whyWrong.C: Is the plural possessive, which would require more than one guild.
whyWrong.D: Is not a standard English form; a plural already ending in s never takes an additional 's.

whyCorrect: The sentence before says Yau's allusions are typically subtle, catchable only by his most attentive readers. The sentence with the blank then reports a poem in which he names his source outright. That is the exception to the pattern, so the transition has to signal contrast.

whyWrong.B: Says the explicit naming suits expectations, but it runs against the habit just described.
whyWrong.C: Marks likeness, and an explicit identification is the opposite of a subtle gesture.
whyWrong.D: Would present the poem as an instance of the subtle pattern, when it is the case that breaks it.

whyCorrect: The first sentence establishes a pattern — many adjectives share a root with their nouns, as "monetary" does with "money." The sentence with the blank states that some adjectives do not. The second statement cuts against the first, so a contrast transition is needed; the "bovine"/"cow" pair that follows is the example of the exception.

whyWrong.A: Signals what happened next in time, but the two sentences describe two categories of words, not a sequence of events.
whyWrong.B: Asserts that the second sentence follows from the first, when it actually limits it.
whyWrong.D: Would introduce a narrowing of the first claim, and exceptions to a pattern are not a specification of that pattern.

whyCorrect: The first half of the sentence describes votes being cast for parties and then tabulated; the half after the blank describes seats being handed out in proportion to those totals. The seat allocation follows directly from the tabulation, so the transition has to mark that result.

whyWrong.A: Would require an explicit "first of all" earlier, and the passage numbers nothing; it describes a process, not a list.
whyWrong.B: Signals emphasis or a surprising confirmation, but the seat allocation is simply the next consequence of the count.
whyWrong.C: Sets up an opposition, and the two halves of the sentence are consecutive stages of one procedure rather than opposites.

whyCorrect: The goal asks for an example of a specimen's nickname, so the sentence has to contain an actual nickname. Only one option supplies it: Roberta, identified as the nickname of a Brachylophosaurus specimen at the Great Plains Dinosaur Museum and Field Station.

whyWrong.A: Says nicknames are given and points to a museum but never states what the nickname is.
whyWrong.B: Reports two general facts about fossil specimens and names no specimen at all.
whyWrong.D: Describes the specimen's genus, period, and location while leaving out the one detail the goal requires.

whyCorrect: To emphasize a difference, the sentence must attach a distinct detail to each piece. Only one option does: Katcina Dances draws on traditional Hopi songs while Fantasy Aborigine No. 3 uses a Tewa seashell rattle, with the contrast marked by "while."

whyWrong.A: Groups the two pieces as works by the same composer, which is a similarity and gives no detail about either.
whyWrong.B: Explicitly treats the two together, blending the same categories of element, so the difference between them disappears.
whyWrong.C: Mentions different approaches in the abstract but never says which piece uses songs and which uses an instrument.

whyCorrect: The goal asks for one public service Ixmiquilpan is responsible for, so the sentence has to name a service. The notes supply exactly one — water treatment — and only one option states it while connecting it to Ixmiquilpan's status as a municipality.

whyWrong.B: Says the municipalities provide public services but never specifies which service, so no example is given.
whyWrong.C: Also stops at "public services" in general and spends the rest of the sentence on location.
whyWrong.D: Reports population figures, which have nothing to do with the services the municipality provides.

whyCorrect: The colon means what follows explains the blank, and what follows is a run of unlike sources — a folk tune, a hymn, and a march — packed into two minutes of one movement. The word has to describe music assembled from widely varied styles.

whyWrong.A: Means held back or understated, which conflicts with three contrasting quotations crowded into a short span.
whyWrong.C: Would call for the same material returning; the passage lists three different kinds of material instead.
whyWrong.D: Describes mood, and the mix of a folk tune, a hymn, and a march says nothing about how dark the music is.

whyCorrect: The sentence is the summary — "In short" — of the argument just made: historical understanding is central to grasping state politics, and a functioning citizenry cannot leave it to experts. Both halves of the summary must run the same direction, so the blank has to deny that historical knowledge is an unnecessary extra. Superfluous is that word.

whyWrong.A: Turns the claim into one about difficulty. The argument is that history matters to everyone, not that ordinary people are able to learn it.
whyWrong.C: Would say historical knowledge is rare, which clashes with the second half about not leaving it to historians alone.
whyWrong.D: Applies fairness to a body of knowledge, which does not fit the grammar of the sentence or the argument being summarized.

whyCorrect: The evidence after the colon is a ranking: "iloveyou" was the eighth most commonly used password in 2019. That is a fact about how many people choose it, so the blank must describe the widely chosen approach — the one most users take, not the one experts recommend.

whyWrong.A: "iloveyou" is offered as an obvious, easily remembered choice, which is the opposite of inventive.
whyWrong.C: Contradicts the sentence, which says this approach favors convenience over security; complicated passwords are what the experts urge.
whyWrong.D: Says nothing about how many people use the approach, and the evidence given is a popularity ranking.

whyCorrect: The fact that follows the blank — that the features enabling flight limit top speed less than those suited to swimming — is the cause, and the speed gap between the eagle and the swordfish is what results from it. So the blank has to name the gap as an effect: it is largely a consequence of that fact.

whyWrong.B: Would make the speed difference something aimed at, but neither animal is pursuing a target speed.
whyWrong.C: Means a rejection, which would put the speed difference at odds with the stated fact rather than following from it.
whyWrong.D: Reverses the direction. The fact about flight and swimming explains the difference; the difference does not explain the fact.

whyCorrect: The first sentence reports critics praising both films, calling one "galvanizing" and the other "exuberant." The blank refers back to that praise, and the fans hope it will draw new viewers. A word meaning enthusiastic public praise is what fits.

whyWrong.A: Means neutrality. The critics are not withholding judgment; they are recommending the films warmly.
whyWrong.B: Means mixed feelings, but both quoted words are unambiguously positive.
whyWrong.C: Means the ability to anticipate the future, which is not what the critics displayed in praising two existing films.

whyCorrect: The text gives two reasons scholars care about juvenilia. Unpublished early work by writers who later became famous, like Auden's "Autumn," shows how those writers developed; and work by lesser-known writers, like Ashford's widely read novels, matters for understanding literary history. Both halves are justifications for studying the material, which is the text's purpose.

whyWrong.A: No publishing difficulties are described. Auden's poem is simply noted as unpublished, with no account of any attempt to publish it.
whyWrong.B: Never ranks the two writers. Ashford's novels are said to deserve attention, not to be better than Auden's early work.
whyWrong.C: Involves no comparison between young writers and adults writing at the same time; the comparison drawn is between famous and lesser-known juvenilia.

whyCorrect: The text sets up two traditions — tightly controlled private collections in the republic, then public libraries from 28 BCE — and the last sentence turns on "however" to collapse the distinction. Fernandes's point is that emperor and private owner alike treated their libraries as extensions of personal patronage, differing only in scale. Establishing that underlying likeness is what the text exists to do.

whyWrong.A: Public access is precisely what the republican period lacked, and the text runs past that period into the imperial libraries.
whyWrong.B: Makes no complaint about imperial power; patronage is described, not criticized.
whyWrong.D: Nothing is said about private libraries ceasing to exist, so there is no such notion for the text to question.

whyCorrect: The narrator calls it "happy" for Barton that he did not overhear his neighbors, then asks whether any of us would be more satisfied for having compared our own picture of our doings with the picture in our neighbors' minds. The closing image answers it: we are plants held up by "the air-vessels of our own conceit," and a few pinches that let the air out would take away even our capacity for good. Ignorance of that gap is presented as a protection.

whyWrong.A: Introduces honesty and the reluctance to confront others, but the passage is about what a person would learn about himself, not about anyone deciding whether to speak up.
whyWrong.B: Misreads the pinches. They deflate self-regard, and the loss described is the capacity for good, not a wish to appear considerate.
whyWrong.C: Reverses the point. The passage does not accuse people of dwelling on others' opinions; it suggests they are fortunate not to know them.

whyCorrect: Each speaker tries to "hew out his conception of art a little more clearly" with what amounts to an ill-balanced axe, and sits down sensing that "for some reason which he could not grasp, his strokes had gone awry." That is failure to make the vision coherent, combined with not understanding the cause of the failure.

whyWrong.A: Gets the private half backwards: after sitting down they immediately turn to a neighbor to rectify and continue what they said, so private talk is what they prefer.
whyWrong.C: Attributes contempt for the others, which never appears; the speakers' dissatisfaction is with their own attempts.
whyWrong.D: No question is posed to the group. Each person is trying to articulate his own conception, not searching for an answer to something asked.

whyCorrect: The hypothesis is comparative: in low visibility, wider-headed fish should detect obstructions less often than narrower-headed fish. Support therefore needs two species of different head widths tested under the same conditions, with the wider-headed one performing worse. The bristlemouth colliding more often than the dusky smooth-hound, with medium-sized vortices and low visibility, is exactly that comparison.

whyWrong.A: Compares individuals within one narrow-headed species, so head width is held constant and the hypothesis is never tested.
whyWrong.C: Reports equal collision rates for the two head shapes, which counts against the hypothesis rather than for it.
whyWrong.D: Gives a figure for the wide-headed species alone. Without a narrow-headed comparison, more than half tells you nothing about relative ability.

whyCorrect: Follow the chain the text sets up: larger body size means longer life span, and wing centroid size stands in for body size. So the illustration has to show larger wings in a warmer month than in a cooler one. July, with an average high of 87°F, gives an average male wing size of 2.02 mm against October's 1.98 mm at 67°F.

whyWrong.A: Compares only temperatures. With no wing measurement it says nothing about body size or life span.
whyWrong.C: Misreports the table: the average female wing size in July is 2.31 mm, not 2.02 mm, and June's figure is also 2.31 mm, so no difference would remain anyway.
whyWrong.D: Compares females with males in the same months, which is a difference between the sexes rather than between warmer and cooler months.

whyCorrect: The researcher's argument is that Garrod chose the women deliberately, judging them better at delicate work — as against the rival account that she simply had no men available. A notebook entry saying she set the women to sieving because their touch was surer than any labourer she could train, and that she meant to keep them at it, states both the judgment and the intention.

whyWrong.A: Supports the opposing explanation: it says she turned to women only because the men were busy with the harvest.
whyWrong.C: Concerns weather and trench conditions and mentions no workers at all.
whyWrong.D: Points to cost as the reason for hiring many hands, which is another practical motive rather than a judgment about skill.

whyCorrect: The findings are that red is associated with power and dominance and can prompt caution and hesitation. Applied to soccer, that means opponents facing Liverpool's mainly red home kit could have responded to the color itself, which fits Liverpool's stronger home record against a club whose kit is not red. The conclusion the evidence supports is that the opponents may have been influenced by the color.

whyWrong.A: Runs against the cited research, which links red to caution and hesitation rather than aggression, and it adds a comparison to the opponents' own uniform color that the text never raises.
whyWrong.C: Requires the players to have recognized the effect. The findings describe an influence on behavior, not awareness of it.
whyWrong.D: Shifts to what the fans were wearing, which the text does not mention, and asserts no effect where the passage is building toward one.

whyCorrect: Two facts do the work: ravens eat finch eggs, and they spot nests near open roadside more easily than nests buried in woodland. Nests near the new road are therefore easier for ravens to find, so those nests should lose eggs at a higher rate than the ones deeper in the trees.

whyWrong.A: Predicts no change in the ravens' overall diet, which is a claim about the predators' feeding across all food sources rather than about which finch nests are at risk.
whyWrong.B: Predicts finches will move toward the danger. Nothing in the text suggests finches respond to raven pressure by nesting nearer the road.
whyWrong.D: Concerns clutch size. The passage describes nests being found and eggs eaten, not how many eggs finches lay.

whyCorrect: Two complete clauses meet here: "the air temperature was 16°C at site CC1, the site with the highest elevation" and "it had shifted to 16.8°C by 11:00 p.m." Joining them requires both a comma and a coordinating conjunction, and that same comma closes the appositive naming CC1 as the highest site.

whyWrong.A: Supplies the conjunction but no comma, so the appositive is never closed and two independent clauses run together without punctuation.
whyWrong.B: Leaves out both the comma and the conjunction, fusing the clauses.
whyWrong.C: Uses a comma alone between two independent clauses, which is a comma splice.

whyCorrect: Each side of the blank is a full sentence: the exhibition "set out to provide a wide-ranging overview of photography by women in the 1920s through the 1950s," and "given the collection's breadth of more than 120 photos, its efforts were largely successful." Two independent clauses joined without a semicolon need a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, which is what the comma and and supply.

whyWrong.A: Uses a comma with no conjunction, leaving a comma splice between the two clauses.
whyWrong.B: Provides no punctuation at all, so the clauses fuse.
whyWrong.C: Supplies the conjunction but drops the comma that is required before it when it joins two independent clauses.

whyCorrect: "Many are still well known" is a complete statement, and what follows illustrates it: Koulsy Lamko, a celebrated playwright from Chad. A colon is the mark that introduces an example after a complete sentence, and it makes the relationship between the two halves explicit.

whyWrong.A: Joins two independent clauses with a comma, producing a splice.
whyWrong.C: Adds and without a comma and treats the example as a second, parallel fact rather than as the illustration it is.
whyWrong.D: Runs the two clauses together with no punctuation.

whyCorrect: Look at what the second half needs: "studying one species recorded emission that varied by less than a tenth" has a participial phrase and the verb recorded, but no one to do the recording. Supplying Researchers as a new subject fixes that, and the period keeps the two complete statements apart.

whyWrong.A: Leaves the second half without a subject, so the participial phrase dangles and recorded has no one performing it.
whyWrong.C: Supplies the subject but joins two independent clauses with only a comma, which is a splice.
whyWrong.D: Supplies the subject with no punctuation between the clauses, fusing them.

whyCorrect: The empire is placed between roughly 600 CE and 1200 CE, and the surrounding verbs are past — the empire reigned, trade was vital, the people received spices and silk in exchange. The simple past produced is the form that matches.

whyWrong.A: The present progressive puts the activity in progress now, which contradicts a civilization that ended in the thirteenth century.
whyWrong.B: The simple present describes a current or habitual action, again clashing with the stated dates.
whyWrong.D: Places the production in the future, which cannot be reconciled with an empire described entirely in the past tense.

whyCorrect: The sentence is inverted: it opens with the prepositional phrase "Among the instruments recovered from the shipwreck," so the subject comes after the verb. That subject is "a brass astrolabe," which is singular, and the recovery is a past event, so the verb is was.

whyWrong.A: Plural, agreeing with instruments inside the opening phrase rather than with the actual subject.
whyWrong.C: Also plural, and the present perfect does not fit a completed past recovery.
whyWrong.D: Plural and present tense, wrong on both counts.

commonMistakes: Treating the noun in the introductory phrase as the subject; in an inverted sentence the subject follows the verb.

whyCorrect: The main verb of the sentence is relied, and its subject is Cartographers. That means the blank cannot hold a second conjugated verb; it needs a participle that modifies the subject. "Cartographers mapping the coastline before satellite imagery existed relied on chains of triangles" gives one subject and one main verb.

whyWrong.B: Creates two finite verbs, mapped and relied, with no conjunction between them.
whyWrong.C: Has the same double-verb problem and also shifts to the present, which clashes with the era before satellite imagery.
whyWrong.D: Also leaves the sentence with two conjugated verbs and no way to connect them.

whyCorrect: The passage is stepping through a procedure. The word first in the previous sentence starts the sequence with building and coating the wax model, and the sentence with the blank gives the following step, melting the wax out. A transition that advances to the next stage is what fits.

whyWrong.A: Signals a summary, but melting out the wax is a new action rather than a recap of the previous one.
whyWrong.C: Sets up a comparison, and no two things are being weighed against each other here.
whyWrong.D: Dismisses an obstacle or objection, and nothing in the first sentence stands in the way of the second.

whyCorrect: The first sentence promises "a range of outcomes." The second gives one outcome — many islands became independent nations — and the sentence with the blank gives the opposite one, islands that remain part of the US or of French Polynesia. The blank has to mark that switch to the contrasting case.

whyWrong.A: Would make the Northern Marianas and the Society Islands instances of islands that gained independence, which is exactly what they are not.
whyWrong.B: Claims the second outcome follows logically from the first, but one group's independence does not cause another group's continued attachment.
whyWrong.C: Signals emphasis or confirmation of the previous statement, when the sentence in fact qualifies it.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states a general fact: some languages require a speaker to mark how a claim was learned. The second narrows to a single language, Tariana, and shows the verb ending that distinguishes what was seen from what was merely reported. Moving from a general rule to one instance calls for an example transition.

whyWrong.B: Marks a contrast, but the Tariana case confirms the general statement rather than pushing against it.
whyWrong.C: Signals a substitution, and nothing in the first sentence is being replaced.
whyWrong.D: Claims logical consequence, but the existence of the Tariana verb ending is an illustration of the rule, not a deduction from it.

whyCorrect: The goal is sequence, so the sentence has to name both winners and make clear which came first. Reddy in 1994 followed by Blum "later, in 1995" gives both dates and states the order outright.

whyWrong.A: Names both winners but supplies no years, so nothing indicates who won first.
whyWrong.C: Covers Blum alone, and one date cannot establish an order.
whyWrong.D: Covers Reddy alone, with the same problem in reverse.

whyCorrect: The goal singles out one figure, the depth of the main well shaft, so the sentence must lead with that number. Only one option reports it: the shaft descends roughly 300 meters below the surface.

whyWrong.A: Gives the 33-kilometer length, a horizontal measure, and the qanat's location instead of the shaft's depth.
whyWrong.B: Describes qanats generally over 2,500 years and never mentions the Gonabad shaft.
whyWrong.D: Reports that the qanat is still in use and how the water moves, with no depth at all.

whyCorrect: To connect the old settlement to modern Pueblo buildings, the sentence needs something both share. The notes give it: Square Tower House was built primarily of adobe and stone, and buildings in Zuni Pueblo and Isleta Pueblo still incorporate those same materials. Naming that continuity is what links the two.

whyWrong.A: Points out what modern buildings have that Square Tower House lacked, which separates them rather than connecting them.
whyWrong.C: Misstates the notes: the contemporary elements belong to modern Pueblo buildings, not to a settlement abandoned around 1300 CE.
whyWrong.D: Stays entirely with Square Tower House's dates and disuse, so no modern building enters the sentence.

whyCorrect: The chief's name gives something to the people: it "breathes bravery and life / And courage to the tribe." The preposition to is the clue — the movement is outward, from the name to the tribe. Imparts carries that sense of conferring or transmitting a quality.

whyWrong.B: Means gives up or rejects, which would have the chief's name denying the tribe its courage.
whyWrong.C: Means agrees, and a name cannot agree bravery to anyone; the grammar of the line rules it out.
whyWrong.D: Reverses the direction, taking the qualities in rather than giving them to the tribe.

whyCorrect: The clause before the dash explains the design: the permafrost holds the temperature down "even if the cooling system fails." That is a second means of doing the same job as the first, deliberately built in as backup. A design with duplicate safeguards is redundant.

whyWrong.B: Contradicts the requirement that the banks stay viable for decades, which is a demand for permanence.
whyWrong.C: Refers to how little space something takes up, and the passage says nothing about size or layout.
whyWrong.D: Means decorative, but siting a vault in permafrost is a functional safeguard, not an aesthetic flourish.

whyCorrect: The older view was absolute — conservation meant stopping decay, and any change counted as a loss. The newer approaches do not throw that out; they soften it by accepting that some materials were meant to age. Temper here means to make less extreme.

whyWrong.A: Would make the older view stronger, the opposite of what the sentence describes, even though it is a common sense of the word in metalwork.
whyWrong.C: Goes too far. The newer approaches still conserve; they qualify the old principle rather than discard it.
whyWrong.D: Means to foresee, but the sentence describes what the new approaches do to an existing view, not what they predict.

commonMistakes: Choosing the technical sense of a familiar word — tempering steel hardens it, but tempering an opinion softens it.

whyCorrect: The phrase after the comma tells you where the coastlines came from: sailors' recollections "rather than from any survey." Lines drawn from remembered impressions instead of measurement are guesswork, so the blank needs a word meaning based on conjecture.

whyWrong.B: Says the maps carried official standing, but the sentence is about how the coastlines were sourced, and unsurveyed lines are the opposite of authoritative.
whyWrong.C: Would make the coastlines ornament rather than information, and the contrast drawn is with surveying, not with illustration.
whyWrong.D: Means limited or kept from circulation, which conflicts with the maps being "widely copied."

whyCorrect: The colon defines the blank, and what follows is a measurement failure: two clocks in one town drifting fifteen minutes apart within a single day. That is a statement about accuracy, so the blank needs a word meaning inaccurate.

whyWrong.A: Describes decoration. How elaborate a clock case is has no bearing on whether the clock keeps time.
whyWrong.B: Concerns whether a clock can be carried, which the evidence about disagreement never touches.
whyWrong.C: Concerns cost, and the example measures timekeeping error rather than price.

whyCorrect: The first half identifies the collection — 85 essays, three authors, published pseudonymously in New York papers to argue for ratification. The colon in the second half turns to a gap in the record: most essays have settled authorship, but No. 52 might be Hamilton's or Madison's. Introduction followed by an acknowledged uncertainty is the shape of the text.

whyWrong.B: Turns the uncertainty into disagreement among the authors. The essays all argue for ratification; what is unsettled is who wrote which one.
whyWrong.C: Misreads the ambiguity as co-authorship. No. 52 was written by one person; scholars just cannot say which of the two it was.
whyWrong.D: Reverses the order and the emphasis. Publication details come early, and the text closes on the authorship question rather than on publishing history.

whyCorrect: The text builds to Bloom's afterword and then explains what he praises: Little, Big blends Schiller's naive and sentimental modes, showing a work can be both rather than one or the other. Schiller's categories are introduced only to make that grounds for admiration intelligible, so the text's purpose is to give the reason behind a critic's high opinion.

whyWrong.A: Argues the opposite of what the passage says. Schiller's either-or scheme is cited so that the novel can be shown to break it.
whyWrong.B: Merrill is named only as another admirer; his own poetry is never described or set beside Crowley's work.
whyWrong.C: Nothing is said about what prompted Crowley to write the novel, only about what a critic values in it.

whyCorrect: The narrator gives Day the look of importance — features fit for a bust or a stamp, a forehead bulging with grey matter — and then undercuts it. It would be "impertinent to inquire too closely into the actual achievements his half century of public service had produced," and the memoirs bury any answer past page thirty. The appearance of eminence is established; the substance behind it is left open.

whyWrong.A: Nothing dishonorable is reported. The joke is that the memoirs are unreadable enough to leave the question unanswered, not that they expose misconduct.
whyWrong.B: Credits him with capable service and modesty, but the passage withholds any confirmation of achievement and describes a man who looks the part rather than one who avoids notice.
whyWrong.D: Takes "state secrets" literally. The phrase is a jibe at how long the memoirs take to reach any detail, not a claim that his work is classified.

tips: With ironic narration, ask what the narrator implies rather than what the flattering words say on their face.

whyCorrect: Watch what stays fixed and what moves as Harris retells the story. His companion shifts from the captain, to the second mate, to "one other man," to nobody at all — but in every version Harris is among those who were not ill. The constant is his own boast; the details are what he adjusts.

whyWrong.A: No comparison of time spent with passengers and captain appears. The captain figures only as the other person who was not seasick.
whyWrong.B: Harris is not struggling to recall anything, and he volunteers the anecdotes rather than being questioned about a first crossing.
whyWrong.D: Concerns the current trip, but Harris is recounting past crossings and showing off, not expressing worry about the water ahead.

whyCorrect: The claim is that immature females' diets overlap with their mothers' more than immature males' diets do, so the example needs one high overlap figure and one clearly lower one. A mother-offspring overlap of about 81% set against one of about 20% shows that gap plainly, matching the order in which the passage names females before males.

whyWrong.A: Reverses the two figures, so the individual named first would be the one with the low overlap and the example would contradict the sentence it is meant to illustrate.
whyWrong.B: Pairs two high values, roughly 81% and 72%, which are close enough that no contrast between the sexes emerges.
whyWrong.D: Pairs two low values, roughly 16% and 20%, so again neither individual shows the strong overlap the claim requires.

commonMistakes: Picking any pair with a big difference; the larger figure has to belong to the individual the claim predicts will be higher.

whyCorrect: The ecologist has to rule out temperature as the cause, which means finding a case where temperature changed the same way but otters did not come back. If kelp failed to expand along those stretches, the temperature change alone cannot explain the recovery, and the otters' return becomes the difference that matters.

whyWrong.A: Strengthens the rival explanation by giving temperature a direct effect on kelp growth.
whyWrong.C: Fits the proposed chain but does not separate the two candidate causes, since urchin numbers could fall for reasons unrelated to otters.
whyWrong.D: Establishes only how long the otters were gone, which says nothing about why the kelp recovered.

tips: To support one cause over another, look for the comparison that holds the rival cause constant and varies only the proposed one.

whyCorrect: Solà's hypothesis is about an outcome — less severe downstream flooding — so the finding that supports it has to measure flooding itself. Lower peak river levels downstream after reintroduction, compared against storms of similar rainfall before it, tests exactly that while holding the rainfall constant.

whyWrong.A: Answers the critics' point about breaching but stops short of the outcome; dams can be rebuilt quickly and still make no difference downstream.
whyWrong.B: Reports how many beavers were present, which is an input rather than evidence about flood severity.
whyWrong.D: Concerns water clarity, a different variable entirely and unrelated to how much water the dams hold back.

whyCorrect: Gather what the evidence actually shows: the fox lay among human artifacts and may have been deliberately buried, it lived at the site at the same time as the people, and its teeth record a partly plant-based diet unlike the all-meat diet of wild foxes. Living alongside people, eating what they ate, and being buried by them all point to an animal kept in close association with humans.

whyWrong.A: Compares the humans' meat intake with the fox's, but the isotopic evidence establishes only that both diets included plant material, not who ate more of what.
whyWrong.B: Uses the jackal comparison for the wrong purpose. Dusicyon avus is said to resemble a jackal in form, and no jackal diet is described anywhere in the text.
whyWrong.C: Draws a conclusion about human hunting technique. The spear points show human habitation, and nothing in the fox's remains speaks to how the people hunted.

whyCorrect: The one result reported is that wild tucos are most active during the day while captive tucos are not. Since the animals are the same species and only the setting changed, the setting is the likely cause of the difference — the lab is disturbing the very rest-and-activity pattern the researchers wanted to observe.

whyWrong.A: Reverses the conclusion. A setting that changes the behavior being measured is less trustworthy for studying that behavior, not more.
whyWrong.B: Extends the finding to dark-eyed juncos, which are mentioned only as another species that has been studied in both settings; no junco result is given.
whyWrong.C: Ranks the lab's suitability for one species against another, but the text supplies data for tucos alone.

whyCorrect: The list "race, gender, history, and memory" ends at the blank, and what follows — "she is credited with expanding the horizons of conceptual photographic art" — is a complete sentence, as is everything before it. Two independent clauses need a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, so the comma closes the first clause and and joins the second.

whyWrong.B: Supplies the conjunction without the comma required before it when it links two independent clauses.
whyWrong.C: Leaves a comma alone between two complete sentences, which is a splice.
whyWrong.D: Provides no punctuation or conjunction, fusing the two clauses.

whyCorrect: The subject is "The practice of storing grain in raised stone granaries" and the blank holds its verb, with "several communities in the Atlas Mountains" as the object. Subject, verb, and object form one uninterrupted unit, so no punctuation belongs anywhere in it.

whyWrong.B: Puts a comma between the verb and its object, which is never allowed.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and the material before it is only a subject.
whyWrong.D: Separates the subject from its verb with a comma, cutting the sentence at its most basic joint.

whyCorrect: Both halves stand alone: "Sourdough bakers rely on a starter that is never entirely used up" and "a portion is always held back to leaven the next loaf." The second explains how the first is possible, and a colon after a complete sentence is the mark that introduces that explanation.

whyWrong.B: Joins two independent clauses with a comma alone, producing a splice.
whyWrong.C: Adds and but omits the comma required before a coordinating conjunction linking two independent clauses, and it also flattens the explanatory relationship into simple addition.
whyWrong.D: Leaves the clauses fused with no punctuation between them.

whyCorrect: The phrase reads "including the languages Javanese and Bikol": the two names identify which languages are meant, so they attach directly to the noun with nothing between. The sentence's interruption is already marked by the pair of dashes around the whole "including" phrase, and no further punctuation is needed inside it.

whyWrong.B: A colon must follow a complete sentence, and "including the languages" is a fragment of a phrase.
whyWrong.C: Adds a third dash inside a passage already bracketed by a pair, so the reader cannot tell which dash closes the interruption.
whyWrong.D: Sets the names off as though they were nonessential, but they are exactly what specifies which of the 1,200 languages the sentence means.

whyCorrect: What people around the world can access is the historical newspapers, referred to as "these rare items" earlier in the sentence. That antecedent is plural, so the pronoun must be the plural object form them.

whyWrong.A: Is singular and has no singular antecedent; the library itself is not what is being accessed.
whyWrong.C: Is a singular demonstrative and, used alone, points to no specific noun in the sentence.
whyWrong.D: Is also singular and equally vague about what is being accessed.

whyCorrect: The events are anchored in 1783 — the eruption began, it lasted eight months, and the harvests were affected "that year." A completed action in a stated past year takes the simple past, so damaged is the form that fits.

whyWrong.A: The simple present describes habitual or current action, which contradicts a single event in the eighteenth century.
whyWrong.B: The present progressive places the damage in progress now.
whyWrong.D: Puts an event from 1783 in the future, clashing with both the date and the past-tense verbs around it.

whyCorrect: The things surveyors measure individually are the glaciers named in the opening clause, and that noun is plural. The end of the sentence confirms it by setting those separate glaciers against "the range as a single system," so the pronoun has to be the plural them.

whyWrong.A: Is singular, and the only singular candidate is the range — measuring the range individually contradicts the rest of the sentence.
whyWrong.B: Is a singular demonstrative that neither matches a plural antecedent nor points to a specific noun.
whyWrong.C: Is singular as well, and used on its own it leaves the reader unsure what is being measured.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the limiting facts — hand harvesting and only three usable stigmas per flower — and the second gives what those facts add up to: about 150,000 flowers for a kilogram. The second follows from the first, so the transition must mark a result.

whyWrong.A: Signals that something holds despite the previous statement, but the flower count is a direct product of the low yield.
whyWrong.B: Sets two things in opposition, and only one situation is described here.
whyWrong.C: Draws a parallel between comparable cases, when the second sentence is the consequence of the first rather than a match for it.

whyCorrect: The first sentence describes the usual arrangement: the roadway carries the load down to the piers. The second describes the suspension bridge, where the roadway hangs from cables and the load travels upward instead. Same load, opposite direction — the transition has to mark the reversal.

whyWrong.A: Signals likeness, but the two load paths run in opposite directions.
whyWrong.B: Would make the suspension bridge an instance of the usual design, when it is the exception to it.
whyWrong.D: Claims the suspension design follows as an effect of the standard design, and no causal link is stated.

whyCorrect: Each sentence names a separate benefit of a green roof: less stormwater in the drains, and insulation that cuts heating and cooling energy. The second neither restates nor corrects the first — it adds a second advantage, which calls for an additive transition.

whyWrong.A: Signals a condensed restatement, but the insulation point is new information rather than a summary.
whyWrong.B: Marks a replacement, and neither benefit rules out the other.
whyWrong.D: Introduces a time relation the sentences do not have; both effects hold at once.

whyCorrect: To explain the implications, the sentence has to say what the find means for the existing hypothesis, not merely that it means something. The 16,000-year-old tools predate the Clovis arrival by about 3,000 years, so they indicate people were already in North America — which runs against Clovis First. Only one option states that consequence outright.

whyWrong.A: Summarizes the hypothesis and never mentions the Saltville tools, so no implication is drawn.
whyWrong.B: Places Saltville among more than a dozen pre-Clovis sites, which is context rather than a statement of what the discovery implies.
whyWrong.C: Announces that the tools have important implications but never says what they are, leaving the goal unmet.

tips: When a goal asks for implications, the sentence must contain the conclusion itself, not a promise that one exists.

whyCorrect: The goal is a difference in production method, so the sentence needs each script's technique and an explicit contrast. Pressing a reed stylus into wet clay against carving into stone or painting onto plaster supplies both methods, and whereas marks the difference.

whyWrong.A: Reports what the two scripts were used for, a similarity, and says nothing about how either was made.
whyWrong.C: States only that both existed in the ancient world, with no method and no contrast.
whyWrong.D: Discusses the purposes of hieroglyphs and leaves cuneiform out entirely.

whyCorrect: Two constraints shape this one. The audience already knows who Luu is, so introducing her wastes the sentence, and the emphasis must fall on a single discovery, (19308) 1996 TO66. The option that gives that discovery its date and its discoverers, and nothing else, keeps the focus where the goal puts it.

whyWrong.A: Runs both discoveries together in sequence and ends on the 1998 one, so the emphasis lands on the later find.
whyWrong.B: Gives the two discoveries equal weight with "not only … but also," which divides the attention the goal wants concentrated.
whyWrong.C: Spends the sentence identifying Luu for readers who already know her and mentions the minor planet only as one item in a list.
